deep.reconstruction:
Topic: the transformation between ecliptic coordinates (longitude λ, latitude β) and equatorial coordinates (right ascension α, declination δ), with obliquity ε. Gauss then finds how α and δ change when λ changes and β stays fixed. Read physically, this is a star's ecliptic longitude increasing through general precession, so the page derives the classical precession formulas in α and δ.

(0) The sketch is a spherical triangle with sides marked 90−λ and 90+α. These are complements of the coordinates, the usual way to set up the triangle formed by the poles and the star.

(1) cos α cos δ = cos λ cos β. Both sides equal the x-coordinate of the star's unit vector; the x-axis points to the equinox and is shared by both frames.

(2) sin δ = cos ε sin β + sin ε cos β sin λ. This is the z-coordinate after rotating by ε about the x-axis.

(3) Inverse relation: sin β = cos ε sin δ − sin ε cos δ sin α. The second term as written on the page or in the transcription appears garbled; see the corrections.

(4) cos ε sin λ = tan β sin ε + tan α cos λ. This is the four-part (cotangent) formula. It follows from cos δ sin α = cos β sin λ cos ε − sin β sin ε, after dividing by cos β cos λ = cos δ cos α.

(5) The inverse four-part formula: −cos ε sin α = tan δ sin ε − tan λ cos α. It follows from cos β sin λ = cos δ sin α cos ε + sin δ sin ε, divided by cos δ cos α.

(6) Differentiate (2) with β held constant: cos δ dδ = sin ε cos β cos λ dλ. Hence dδ/dλ = sin ε cos β cos λ / cos δ. Using (1) this becomes dδ/dλ = sin ε cos α.

(7) Differentiate (4) with β held constant: cos ε cos λ dλ = (cos λ / cos²α) dα − tan α sin λ dλ. Gauss writes the tan α sin λ term on the left side: cos ε cos λ + tan α sin λ = (cos λ/cos²α) dα/dλ.

(8) Solving (7): dα/dλ = cos²α cos ε + cos α sin α tan λ.

(9) Multiply (5) by −sin α (this step is mine, but implicit on the page). This gives cos α sin α tan λ = cos ε sin²α + tan δ sin ε sin α.

(10) Substituting (9) into (8): dα/dλ = cos ε (cos²α + sin²α) + sin ε tan δ sin α = cos ε + sin ε tan δ sin α.

Result: with dλ = p (general precession in longitude),
- dα = p (cos ε + sin ε sin α tan δ)
- dδ = p sin ε cos α

In the classical notation m = p cos ε, n = p sin ε, this is dα = m + n sin α tan δ and dδ = n cos α.
errors: No genuine mathematical errors in the chain; every final result checks.

Line 3 as transcribed ('cos ε sin δ − cos ε sin δ sin α') is wrong. The correct inverse formula is sin β = cos ε sin δ − sin ε cos δ sin α. The slip is either Gauss's (ε and δ interchanged in the second term) or the transcription's; it is not used later.
In the dα step the term tan α sin λ is written on the left-hand side with a + sign. This is correct as a rearrangement, but it is easy to misread as part of the right side.
The differentials are written loosely: 'dδ = ...' means dδ/dλ at constant β. This is notational, not an error.

results.what: Ecliptic–equatorial transformation formulas: cos α cos δ = cos λ cos β; sin δ = cos ε sin β + sin ε cos β sin λ; and the inverse
results.modern_name: Ecliptic to equatorial coordinate transformation (rotation about the equinox axis by the obliquity)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical spherical astronomy (Ptolemy onward; modern form Euler/Lagrange era)

results.what: cos ε sin λ = tan β sin ε + tan α cos λ and −cos ε sin α = tan δ sin ε − tan λ cos α
results.modern_name: Four-part (cotangent) formula of spherical trigonometry applied to the polar triangle

results.what: dα/dλ = cos ε + sin ε sin α tan δ, dδ/dλ = sin ε cos α (β fixed)
results.modern_name: Annual precession in right ascension and declination: m + n sin α tan δ, n cos α
results.usually_credited_to: 18th-century astronomy (Bradley, Euler, Lalande, Lagrange); standard in textbooks

deep.surprise_reason: These are textbook spherical-astronomy formulas: the coordinate transformation and the standard precession formulas, derived in a routine way. They were well known before and during Gauss's time.

checkable.asserts: cos ε sin λ = tan β sin ε + tan α cos λ, with tan α = (cos β sin λ cos ε − sin β sin ε)/(cos β cos λ); should simplify to 0

Inverse four-part formula. With cos δ sin α = cos β sin λ cos ε − sin β sin ε and sin δ = cos ε sin β + sin ε cos β sin λ, the identity cos β sin λ = cos ε cos δ sin α + sin ε sin δ holds, which is equivalent to −cos ε sin α = tan δ sin ε − tan λ cos α; should simplify to 0
Corrected inverse formula sin β = cos ε sin δ − sin ε cos δ sin α; should simplify to 0
dδ/dλ at constant β equals sin ε cos α
dα/dλ at constant β equals cos ε + sin ε tan δ sin α; check numerically if simplify stalls
Final algebraic step: cos²α cos ε + cos ε sin²α + tan δ sin ε sin α = cos ε + sin ε tan δ sin α

transcription_corrections: Line 3: the second term of the inverse formula should read sin ε cos δ sin α, not cos ε sin δ sin α. Correct formula: sin β = cos ε sin δ − sin ε cos δ sin α. A crossed-out start ('cos ...') precedes 'sin β'.

In the second line of the dα block, the uncertain symbol '[-=-]' is a struck-through '=', and the line reads cos ε sin²α = cos α sin α tg λ (with + tang δ sin ε sin α on the next line), i.e. cos α sin α tan λ = cos ε sin²α + tan δ sin ε sin α.
'+ tang α sin λ' belongs to the left-hand side: cos ε cos λ + tang α sin λ = (cos λ / cos²α) dα.
'cos α²' and 'sin α²' denote cos²α and sin²α (Gauss's usual notation).
